2131944687095283942: 01. Night of the Majestic Cosmos: The Dawn of Dreams & Freedom Author: Louis Rice As the opening chapter in this series of criticisms, the work I have selected is Night of the Majestic Cosmos. This is an iconic work from the famous painter Sharlotte's early life, and is also where the title of this series of notes takes its name. Just like their other early works, this painting has yet to receive the acclaim and praise it deserves to this day because it has not yet showcased the artist's unique dreamy kaleidoscopic style. I wish to express my deepest regret for this. Let us first consider the painting itself: Beneath a vast and brilliant starry sky, a black lighthouse symbolizing human civilization and order looks frail and insignificant — like a small boat drifting in a boundless ocean. All it would take is a single storm or a lone tidal wave to completely wipe any trace of its existence from the face of the earth. And the composition of this image uses exaggerated lines that are perpetually flowing like a spiral. These lines devour everything like frothing waves, spinning, agitating, and upheaving, constructing everything while deconstructing everything. As for technique, the artist's brushwork at this time was still a little underdeveloped, with a still immature palette. And compared to the dreamy style of later works, it is obviously too "conservative and photo-realistic." However, from this painting, we can easily glimpse into the artist's reflections on "people" and "the world." "When we look up to the stars, what are we looking at?" Every time we look up and gaze out at the vast and inscrutable universe, we are inevitably faced with our own insignificance. Humans — or rather, all civilizations of intelligent life — are nothing more than a fleeting and fragile candle flame before the unfathomable and mysterious might of nature. However, in this painting, all phenomena in the world — be it the eternal night sky, the boundless universe, the insignificant lighthouse symbolizing humanity, or the shaft of light beamed out from that lighthouse — are fundamentally just twisted lines randomly doodled by Imaginary Law. We come from the stars, and are no different to space dust. Everything in this world is ultimately meaningless. So, in this cold and empty tone, what answer has our painter given us? Take a look at the mysterious violet tones dotted into the indigo night sky. The constellations are giving off these gentle pale yellow lights. These lights contrast and harmonize with the flame in the lighthouse, so we feel the restless joy of time passing, but also warmth ignited in this cold long night. Thanks to these colors, those messy and restless lines no longer look cold and ruthless because they are faithful to nature. They still flow — looping back and forth, never stopping — but they emanate a gentle halo due to having been stained by the warmth of human souls, bringing a touch of life to the vast and empty night sky. Even if reality is nothing more than a dream... Even if the universe was not created for humanity... We still need to pursue the sky that belongs exclusively to ourselves — be it in a painting, or in our dreams.

There he lights flame with blood, and blood with flame, like a sun whose blaze banished all evil from its path.
The mountains rise cruel and steep. Yet still he dances there alone, wild and unceasing in his joy.

8164705121301676262: He still remembered those early days in the Zhuming, gazing up at the endless shelves of forging manuals, the armory's display of divine weapons stretching out like an endless sea. As a mayfly never sees the night, a cicada knows nothing of spring and autumn. For the first time in his life, he truly understood how small a man could be next to the ages. With the short lifespan of his kind, he'd be lucky to even scratch the surface of the forging art. He could only start from scraps, filling the crumbling smelting furnace with coal slag. He failed. That sword seemed flawless and sharp beyond measure, yet shattered into pieces when he flicked his finger to test it. "A useless blade..."Burning with shame, he hid it away. What he didn't see was his white-haired master running a finger across that broken sword, nor the thin red line of blood it left on his fingertip. "Waste not the bounty of the world, but perfect it through craft. Good." He remembered the shackles he forged for the Ten-Lords Commission. "Forging a blade is like tempering the soul. The real skill is making the simplest thing well." He didn't understand. If his skills were already exceptional, why did his master make him start from being an apprentice? But he never argued. He believed in the general's words, just as he believed that a true gem never stays buried for long. His fellow disciples came, the Flamewheel Octet came, Huaiyan came. They all watched him, laboring day and night without rest in the Forge. Until the flames finally died out, and they laid eyes on the most fearsome shackles of their lives. The cold gleam of those manacles was muted, but their menace weighed on one like a mountain. No one could have imagined that years later, the imprisoned Borisin Warhead would spend long, long years locked up in chains cut from the same cloth. He remembered the trial for Furnace Master. But for a short-life species to be chosen as the chief craftsman of the Zhuming, that was unprecedented. He'd prepared himself well. But when the smelting began, he found that all his materials had been swapped for rotten scrap. He just smiled. A day and a night later, he unveiled a delicate, ingenious mechanical lion, a creation that put any treasure-forged contraption to shame. He remembered how before being granted the title "Furnace Master," his master repeated that simplest of questions— "What makes a blade?" He'd never once hesitated in his answer. That was the peerless weapon he was meant to forge, the one that would leave every other blade in the dust. Yet when these distant memories resurface, all he could hear was the mournful howls of shattered blades.
